title: The King Enters, the Temple Judged, a Fig Tree Withers
summary: Jesus rides into Jerusalem on a colt while crowds shout Hosanna and bless the coming kingdom of David. The next day he curses a leafy fig tree without fruit, drives the traders from the temple courts, and quotes the prophets against the temple's keepers. When the disciples see the fig tree withered, he teaches them about faith, prayer, and forgiveness, and when the temple authorities challenge his authority he answers with a question about John the Baptist that they refuse to answer.
story: The road that began at Caesarea Philippi ends here. Everything from this chapter to the end of Mark happens in and around Jerusalem in about a week, and Mark marks the days carefully. Jesus arrives as the Son of David whom Bartimaeus hailed at Jericho, but his first act in the city is quiet: he enters the temple, looks around at everything, and leaves. The next day he returns and acts. The confrontation with the temple leadership that fills chapters 11 and 12 begins here, and verse 18 states its outcome in advance: the chief priests and scribes look for a way to kill him.
historical:
Bethphage and Bethany were villages on the eastern slope of the Mount of Olives, the ridge that overlooks Jerusalem and the temple from across the Kidron Valley. Bethany, about two miles from the city, served as Jesus' lodging during the week. The Mount of Olives had prophetic weight: Zechariah 14:4 pictures the Lord standing on it on the day he comes to save and judge.

The temple Jesus entered was Herod the Great's rebuilding of the second temple, begun around 20 BC and still being finished. Its vast outer court, the only part open to Gentiles, held the trade needed for worship. Pilgrims bought animals and birds for sacrifice, and money changers exchanged coins from many lands into the Tyrian silver used for the temple tax, since the law required that sacrifices be without blemish and the tax be paid in a specified coin. The temple was run by the high priest and the chief priests, who kept order under Roman oversight and drew wealth from the system. Some historians connect the trade in the courts with arrangements made by the high priestly family, but the details are uncertain. What is clear is that Jesus' action struck at the heart of the institution that held religious and economic power in Judea.
cultural:
A colt on which no one had ever sat was fit for a sacred purpose; the Old Testament set apart unworked animals for holy use (Numbers 19:2, 1 Samuel 6:7). Kings in Israel rode donkeys and mules (1 Kings 1:33), and Zechariah 9:9 pictures Zion's king coming humble on a colt, though Mark does not quote it. Spreading cloaks on the road was a royal welcome (2 Kings 9:13). The crowd's cries come from Psalm 118, sung by pilgrims at the great feasts: Hosanna, originally a plea meaning save now, had become a cry of praise, and “Blessed is He who comes in the name of the Lord” was the psalm's blessing on those who came to the temple. The crowd adds a line about the kingdom of our father David, revealing their hope for a restored Davidic kingdom.

Fig trees near Jerusalem put out leaves in spring, and early small fruit often appeared with or before the leaves, so a tree in full leaf suggested food. Mark's note that it was not the season for figs is a signal that the act is symbolic. The prophets often used fig trees and vines as pictures of Israel and fruitlessness as a picture of judgment (Jeremiah 8:13, Hosea 9:10, Micah 7:1). Prayer in Jesus' day was commonly offered standing, which is why verse 25 speaks of standing to pray.
literary: Mark frames the temple action with the fig tree, another of his sandwiches: the curse (verses 12 to 14), the temple (15 to 19), and the withered tree (20 to 21). Each half explains the other. The tree is all leaves and no fruit, and so is the temple system in Jesus' judgment. Mark alone keeps the full quotation of Isaiah 56:7, “My house will be called a house of prayer for all the nations,” which highlights that the court where Gentiles could pray had been turned into a marketplace. The second quotation, “a den of robbers,” comes from Jeremiah 7:11, where Jeremiah stood in the temple gate and warned that the building would not protect a people who did injustice. The chapter closes with a debate in the form common in Jewish teaching, a question answered by a counter-question. The leaders' reasoning is exposed to the reader in verses 31 and 32, and their answer, we do not know, is a refusal to decide rather than ignorance.

outline.t: Jesus curses the fruitless fig tree
The withered fig tree: faith, prayer, and forgiveness

doctrines.note: The fig tree and the temple action together are a prophetic announcement of judgment on a religious center that looked flourishing but bore no fruit. Jesus stands in the line of Jeremiah, who warned that God would not spare a temple whose worshipers trusted the building and ignored justice.

Jesus calls the temple a house of prayer for all nations and then teaches his disciples to pray with faith and to forgive when they pray. As the temple's role is called into question, the chapter points to a people whose prayer depends on faith in God, not on a building.

The entry is a deliberate royal act. Jesus arranges it, receives the crowd's acclamation of David's coming kingdom, and enters the temple as one with authority over it. Yet he comes on a colt, not a warhorse, and the kingdom he brings will be established through his death.

words.note: Lestes, robber or bandit, a word the Jewish historian Josephus also uses for violent rebels. It comes into Jesus' words from Jeremiah 7:11, where a den of robbers is a hideout where thieves feel safe after their crimes. The charge is that the temple had become a refuge for people who treated worship as cover. Mark uses the same word for the men crucified beside Jesus (15:27).

Suke, fig tree. Figs were one of the chief fruits of the land, and sitting under one's own vine and fig tree was a picture of peace and blessing (Micah 4:4). A leafy, fruitless fig tree therefore made a pointed sign, and the prophets had used the same image for an Israel that gave God nothing.

Proseuche, prayer. Isaiah 56:7 promised that foreigners who joined themselves to the Lord would be brought to his holy mountain and that his house would be a house of prayer for all peoples. Jesus holds the temple to that purpose, and then turns at once to teach his disciples about prayer themselves.

Exousia, authority, the right and power to act. The crowds noticed from the start that Jesus taught with authority unlike the scribes (1:22), and he claimed authority to forgive sins (2:10). The leaders' question in verse 28 is the right question, and the rest of Mark answers it.

christ: Jesus enters Jerusalem as its king and the temple as its Lord. Malachi 3:1 had promised that the Lord would suddenly come to his temple, and Mark opened his Gospel by quoting the verse before it about the messenger who prepares the way (1:2). John was that messenger, which is why Jesus answers the question about his authority by pointing to John. In judging the temple, Jesus also prepares for what he will become: the chapter's picture of a house of prayer for all nations is fulfilled in the new people gathered around the risen Christ, whom the New Testament calls God's temple (1 Corinthians 3:16, Ephesians 2:19-22). The king who comes humbly on a colt will be enthroned on a cross, and the temple he judges will be replaced by his own body raised on the third day.

hard.q: Does Jesus promise that anything we ask for in prayer will be ours if we believe hard enough?
hard.a: Verses 23 and 24 are sometimes read as a guarantee that confident faith obtains whatever a person wants, whether health or wealth or success, and that unanswered prayer shows a lack of faith. That reading does not fit the passage or the rest of Scripture. The saying is spoken on the Mount of Olives in sight of the temple mount, and many interpreters think this mountain refers to that mountain: faith in God, not in the temple, can see even the great religious center removed. The promise is framed by faith in God (verse 22), not faith in one's own faith, and it is followed immediately by the command to forgive (verse 25), which ties prayer to the pray-er's own heart and relationships. Elsewhere Jesus teaches his disciples to pray your will be done, and in Gethsemane he asks for the cup to pass and submits when it does not (14:36). The New Testament also shows faithful people whose requests were refused, like Paul with his thorn (2 Corinthians 12:7-9). Jesus' words teach bold and expectant prayer, trusting that nothing is too hard for God, but they are not a technique for controlling him, and they give no support to the prosperity teaching that treats God as a source of personal gain.

questions: The crowd welcomed Jesus as the bringer of David's kingdom but had their own ideas about what that kingdom would be. What do you hope Jesus will do for you that may not be what he came to do?
The fig tree had leaves and no fruit. Where might your own spiritual life or your church look healthy from a distance and give God little up close?
Jesus ties prayer to forgiveness. Is there someone you need to forgive before you can pray with a clear heart?
